To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) smoking prevalence among Latinos is higher than among non-Latino whites; 2) smoking prevalence among Latino men and women is lower than among non-Latinos; 3) smoking prevalence is higher among men than among women; 4) smoking prevalence is lower among individuals with higher levels of education; 5) smoking prevalence is highest among individuals who have not completed high school; 6) nicotine dependence is higher among men and women than among non-smoking men and women

smoking prevalence among Latinos in California is higher for males than for females, for individuals with less education and for individuals of higher level of accultulation than for individuals of lower level of accultulturation.
smoking prevalence and nicotine dependency among Latinos are higher for men than women, and higher for Latinos with low level of acculuturation than for Latinos with high level of accultration.

the identification of factors associated with smoking behavior among Latinos and other ethnic and gender groups in California.
the health of the Latino population, and it contributes to the literature on the health of this population in the United States.
the development of a conceptual and empirical framework for the study of health behavior and health status in Latinos, and in particular, with the study of smoking behavior and nicotine dependence.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

smoking prevalence among Latinos is high, and that smoking prevalence and nicotine dependency are higher for men than for woman, for individuals who did not finish high school, for Latinos of high acculturation when contrasted with Latinos of low acculturation.

smoking is a serious public health problem among Latinos in California and that smoking prevalence and nicotine addiction is highest among Latinos of low acculturation and among Latinos who have not finished High School.
smoking among Latino men is a serious problem and that smoking prevention programs should be developed for Latinos of low acculturation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
smoking is a problem for Latinos and that the problem is not uniform among Latinos, but rather that it is more severe for some subgroups of Latinos than others.

the prevalence of smoking among Latino men and women is high and that the prevalence and nicotine dependence are higher among Latino men with low levels of education and low levels of acculturation, suggesting that interventions to prevent smoking uptake are most needed for these individuals.

the Latino population is not a homogenous group and that differences in smoking prevalence, nicotine dependence and other smoking-related behaviors are observed among Latino men and women, among Latinos with different levels of acculturation and among Latinos with different level of education.
